text.text: Cervical cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women in 26 countries, including in sub-Saharan African countries.
Cervical and other cancer risks can be greatly reduced through timely HPV vaccination and early screening.
But it continues to pose a significant public health challenge in LMICs such as
Nigeria.

This study reports on the implementation and evaluation of a pair of social media behavior change campaigns to increase HPV vaccination amongst girls ages 9-14 and reduce vaccine hesitancy amongst girls and their parents in Bauchi state, Nigeria.

The primary objectives are to conduct a quasiexperimental evaluation of the social media campaign; to examine the effect of higher versus lower levels of campaign exposure on HPV vaccination and related outcomes; to determine whether the social media campaign followed its planned theory of change; and to identify which social media messages were most effective in promoting HPV vaccination.

We implemented an HPV vaccination social media promotion campaign, using videos designed to encourage parents to vaccinate their daughters, at scale in Bauchi state on the Meta and TikTok social media platforms.
We used a quasi-experimental design, a heavy-up approach, that experimentally manipulated the level of social media content delivered in Bauchi.

We used the Virtual Lab platform, an open-source platform that uses social media to recruit participants using advertising and creates panels of respondents for data collection through an online survey, and also collected social media metrics including impressions and engagement.
The campaign was effective in increasing HPV vaccination rates from 69% at baseline to 86% at endline over 2 campaign phases that spanned approximately 3 months.
Based on GEE modeling, we found that higher levels of engagement with the campaign were associated with higher vaccination rates at midline and endline.
Pro-vaccine attitudes and reduced vaccine hesitancy also predicted higher vaccination rates.

Also, the campaign produced additional HPV vaccinations at low cost: Adjusted for campaign exposure cost of $0.81 per additional vaccination in campaign phase 1, $2.10 per vax in phase 2, and $2.40 for the total campaign period.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that cervical cancer is the fifth most commonly diagnosed cancer in women, with 604,000 new cases estimated in 2024, and that it is the leading cause of cancer death in women in 26 countries, including in sub-Saharan Africa. 1 Lack of systemic Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and screening are a significant contributor to the burden of cancer among women in low and middle income countries (LMIC) generally, and sub-Saharan Africa in particular, 2 unlike in many developed countries.

text.text: There is a specific focus on increasing HPV vaccination rates, and reducing vaccine hesitancy, among 9-14 year-old girls in priority states in Nigeria, including Bauchi state.
As part of this initiative, our research team sought to evaluate the efficacy of social media to increase HPV vaccination rates and reduce vaccine hesitancy in Bauchi state.

The primary objectives to be evaluated in this study are: 1) To conduct a quasi-experimental evaluation of a social media campaign to encourage parents to attend the MNCH week community events in Bauchi state and have their 9-14 year old girls vaccinated for HPV; 2) To examine the effect of higher versus lower levels of campaign exposure on HPV vaccination and related outcomes including social norms and vaccine hesitancy; 3) Determine whether the social media campaign followed its planned theory of change; 4) Identify which social media messages were most effective in promoting vaccination at the MNCH week events and in reducing vaccine hesitancy.

This study employed a quasi-experimental design in which we compared the effects of higher versus lower levels of paid advertising (boosted) social media campaign activity on HPV vaccination outcomes.
This approach, known as a "heavy-up" design in advertising research, has been widely used, including studies in health promotion and public health. 22, 23

text.text: This research, including procedures, instruments, and informed consent form, was reviewed and Participants were contacted through the Meta and TikTok social media platforms through a paid advertising campaign.
Interested participants clicked on a link and were taken to an informed consent form that provided details on the study procedures, delivered through the Facebook Messenger app.
By clicking on an "accept" link after reading the consent, they were entered into a screening protocol for the study.
Participants who were parents of girls age 9-14 and lived in Bauchi state were eligible and offered the survey.
June 2026, we collected survey data from a baseline sample of parents of girls ages 9-14 in Bauchi.
Then we ran the initial social media campaign (phase 1) at a defined level of boosted campaign activity for approximately 4 weeks.
Following this campaign, MNCH week promoting HPV vaccination occurred in early July 2026.
We then collected a 2 nd round of survey data (midline) from the same parents.
Then we ran the campaign at approximately 3 times the level of boosted activity (3 times the advertising spending to generate exposure to content), which included the MNCH week events.
After the end of MNCH week, we collected midline data from the same sample of parents.
We then ran the phase 2 campaign to promote vaccination at other events and activities in Bauchi state in July and August 2026.
The endline survey was conducted immediately after the end of phase 2 in August 2026.
The Bauchi Ministry of Health and local partners, in collaboration with our investigative team, developed social media content in English and Hausa.
Content focused on the benefits of HPV vaccination, and used, in different social media videos, techniques including story telling (narratives), humor, and music.
Attendance at MNCH and opportunities to vaccinate were promoted.
Trusted voices from across Bauchi State were featured in the social media.
Health officials, imams, doctors, mothers, local journalists, poets and comedians all carried the same message: Bring your daughter for a free HPV vaccine.
Inperson outreach events like MNCH Week then turned that intent into action, with free vaccines, free medical care and giveaways at health facilities across the state.
We used a social media campaign management and data collection platform called Virtual Lab to support study implementation.
Virtual Lab was managed by the study team and used to recruit a panel of adult parent participants living in the Bauchi.
The panel was recruited using Meta platform (Facebook and Instagram) paid posts using targeting persona-specific campaigns to survey respondents via remarketing and measure impacts.
We collected a baseline sample of 2,206 individual Bauchi parents who met inclusion criteria.
An online, self-administered survey delivered via the Virtual Lab platform was used for data collection in each identified state.

The survey was designed for completion using Facebook Messenger software (chat feature in which each individual chat contains a survey question), and required approximately 15 minutes to complete at each time point.
We offered participants incentives of 1500 Naira in mobile phone credit per completed survey to maximize completion rates.

Evaluation measures included: demographics (e.g., age, gender, education, work role, income); psychographics (e.g., psychological traits, values, lifestyle variables); vaccination social norms; related vaccine/vaccination beliefs; vaccination history; acceptance/uptake of HPV vaccination; use of social media; exposure to vaccine-specific information (on social media and other sources).
Measures were derived from previous studies by the investigators, and published in the peer-reviewed literature. 18, 20

text.text: Behavior change interventions that rely on social networks for their success are hypothesized to have greater impact than interventions that rely on changes in individual behavior. 24 Thus, in addition to the effect of treatment-on-the-treated, social network researchers have measured the effect of treatment on the untreated.
text.formatted: Behavior change interventions that rely on social networks for their success are hypothesized to have greater impact than interventions that rely on changes in individual behavior. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24</ref> Thus, in addition to the effect of treatment-on-the-treated, social network researchers have measured the effect of treatment on the untreated.

text.text: Researchers who have evaluated door-to-door campaigns to get out the vote, for example, have measured a smaller, discernable effect of such campaigns on the untreated (i.e., effects on members of the household who are not directly exposed to the canvasser).
This additive effect may be due to effects on social norms and other social influences (e.g., based on observation of those who receive treatment by those who do not).
This has implications for cost-effectiveness of social network interventions.
This evaluation examined these potential effects.

The cost to implement a social media campaign to reduce vaccine hesitancy is a key input for future decision-makers considering broader implementation of the strategy following this effectiveness trial.

The goal of the cost-effectiveness analysis component of the evaluation was to quantify the societal costs of implementing the social media campaign and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of the intervention compared to the current standard of care.

We used a micro-costing approach to evaluate resources utilized for all program-related activities using a standard three-stage process of resource identification, measurement, and valuation. 25  The development of a model-based evaluation is beyond the scope of this project; we used a time horizon for the analysis consistent with the intervention time period.

We used bootstrap sampling with replacement from intervention and control groups to estimate 95% uncertainty intervals around ICERs. 26

text.text: We conducted an individual-level power analysis using HPV vaccination rate as the outcome of interest.

Based on this analysis, we concluded that the total sample size required to achieve statistical power of 0.8 for testing the null hypothesis of no difference between the high exposure and low exposure study conditions in self-reported HPV vaccination at a given point in time (follow-up) using a two-sided test resulted in a required sample size of 2,000.
Our final collected baseline sample was 2,206, exceeding power requirements.
The sample was drawn using the Virtual Lab procedures described below.
We sampled from Facebook users who meet eligibility criteria of being a parent with a girl age 9-14 living at home in Bauchi state.
Data collection was conducted by Virtual Lab.
The Virtual Lab is an open-source platform that uses social media such as Facebook and Instagram to recruit participants using advertising and creates panels of respondents for data collection.
The data collection procedures may be summarized as follows.
All data in flight is encrypted via TLS and all data at rest is encrypted on encrypted block storage provided by Google Cloud Services.
Data downloaded by researchers from the web portal is encrypted via TLS to their local machines at which point they must store all data which might contain personal information on encrypted disks.
Respondents can request to see or delete their data at any time by sending an email to an address which is provided to them.
Data deletion requests are handled within 30 days and fully removed from data archives in 60 days after the handling of the deletion request.
Participants were recruited via an ad that is shown both on Facebook and Instagram.
The ad advertised that we want them to take a survey and also explains that they will receive a mobile credit as compensation for their participation.

Ads were targeted to potential respondents via Meta (Facebook and Instagram) targeting demographics including the geographic region in which they live, the industry in which they work (eg, healthcare), their job title, their education, their interests, their age, and their gender.
This targeting was used in the study to ensure representativeness across the desired variables.
On clicking the ad, respondents were directed to a chat window within Facebook Messenger (FM).
This chat window had an initial message which explains again that we would like them to participate in a study and that they will receive mobile credit for participating.
They had the option to click "start" in the chat to start the survey.
Once the respondent clicked "start", Meta sent the Virtual Lab platform a notification that a user with a page-scoped user ID (account) number had started a chat.
This ID was used to identify the user within the Virtual Lab platform and used to communicate with Facebook.
The ID was usable for tracking all user interaction within the chat window and with the page more broadly, but not usable to track user interaction with any other page (thus, it is "page-scoped").
The page-scoped user id was used for "remarketing", by allowing "custom audiences" of 100+ ID's to be created and used for ad targeting.
We used remarketing to test the impact of ad campaigns on "treated" groups of individuals.
For follow-up data collection, participants were sent a message through FM indicating that a new survey was available.
Repeat messages were sent for 7 days until the respondent either completed the survey, or the participant was deemed lost to follow-up.

We used both the survey data and quantitative social media metrics (reach, engagement) data drawn from the Meta platform, capturing views and interactions (likes, comments, shares) with the campaign HPV vaccination posts.
Social media metrics characterize prevention message dissemination, reach, and network engagement, and provide an exogenous measure of participant exposure to content.
Our analysis aimed to isolate the effects of exposure on vaccination and related attitudes and beliefs.
SPSS version 31 was used for all analyses. 27 Based on baseline data, we conducted reliability analyses for all potential scales.

The final total number participants was 546.
Univariate repeated measures analyses were conducted as manipulation checks for the effects of campaign phase on attitude measures, self-reported exposure and vaccine uptake.
The campaign theory of change posits that engagement in the campaign predicts intervention effects on vaccination intentions and uptake.

We calculated a social media engagement variable for use in Generalized estimating equations (GEE) models as an independent variable to capture the effects of the heavy-up design increase in campaign exposure between campaigns 1 and 2.
Attitude measures as defined factor summary scores as well as self-reported exposure were key covariates.

In this project, we implemented an HPV vaccination social media promotion campaign at scale in Bauchi state, Nigeria.
The combined phase 1 and 2 campaigns reached over 1.1 million unique Meta accounts, generated more than 12 million 3-second views, and generated more than 3.1 million full views.

Selfreported exposure, as expected, increased as the 2 campaigns were implemented, from some 69% at baseline (likely due to existing online content related to the HPV vaccine), to nearly 81% at endline.
This suggests that the campaigns not only reached large numbers of people, but that there was increasing awareness and recall of the HPV vaccination promotion messages.
Quasi-experimental evaluation findings, based on the heavy-up design, 22 suggest that the campaign was effective in increasing HPV vaccination rates based on a quasi-experimental evaluation.
text.formatted: Quasi-experimental evaluation findings, based on the heavy-up design, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">22</ref> suggest that the campaign was effective in increasing HPV vaccination rates based on a quasi-experimental evaluation.

text.text: Specifically, in a longitudinal sample, there was an increase in vaccination rates associated with higher levels of engagement with the campaigns.
Engagement was measured through social media metrics, and there were over 825,000 individual engagements (eg, likes, shares, comments) with posts across the phase 1 and 2 campaigns.
However, we did not see a relationship between self-reported recall of campaign posts and higher vaccination rates.
Overall, in our sample, vaccination rates increased from 69% at baseline to 83% and midline and 86% at endline.

We also found that the pro-vaccine attitudes factor, derived from factor analysis of a series of items that asked about and reduced vaccine hesitancy also was associated with higher vaccination rates.

The relationship between positive vaccinated-related attitudes and subsequent vaccination has been examined in recent studies, with mixed results. 29 Researchers have found an attitude-uptake gap in regard to HPV vaccination. 30 Some studies, like ours, have found that substantial increases in provaccine attitudes may be associated with increases in HPV vaccine uptake. 31 But given variable results in such studies, there is no clear evidence base on the role of pro-vaccine attitudes, and related beliefs and intentions, in promoting uptake.

text.text: This area, and how innovative methods such as social media campaigns to promote pro-vaccine attitudes and intentions, calls for more rigorous interventions and research.

Furthermore, we found that the campaign produced additional HPV vaccinations at low cost: Adjusted for campaign exposure cost of $0.81 per additional vax in campaign phase 1, $2.10 per vax in phase 2, and $2.40 for the combined campaigns.

There is limited evidence on the effectiveness of social media campaigns to promote vaccination generally, and HPV vaccination specifically. 32 However, the present study adds to previous research in LMICs that suggests social media is a promising strategy to increase vaccine uptake.

text.text: More rigorous interventions, combined with cost effectiveness analysis, should be conducted to build the evidence base in this area.
Overall, evidence from this study suggests that social media may be an effective strategy to promote HPV vaccination, and that it is cost effective compared to alternatives.

More research is needed on the mechanisms and determinants of HPV vaccine uptake, including the role of psychosocial variables such as vaccine hesitancy, pro-vaccine attitudes, and social norms. 33, 34 Additionally, rigorous study designs, including randomized controlled trials, and dose-response experiments of social media campaigns, are needed to help interpret campaign impact on HPV vaccine uptake and behavioral determinants. 35 Such studies are also needed to build the evidence and allow for valid comparisons between studies on social media vaccination cost effectiveness analysis.

text.text: Overall, this research suggests that future interventions should utilize social media to promote vaccination, and that the types of campaign strategies used in this study may be worth using or adapting.
These include use of storytelling narratives, humor, and messages delivered by trusted and influential voices (social influencers).

While much more evidence is needed on these techniques, other studies have found them to be promising ways to frame health messages, and promote behavior change. 36 Despite the evidence provided by this study, it has some important limitations.
text.formatted: While much more evidence is needed on these techniques, other studies have found them to be promising ways to frame health messages, and promote behavior change. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">36</ref> Despite the evidence provided by this study, it has some important limitations.

text.text: First, we experienced high attrition of approximately 75%.
While attrition is often high in social media-based studies, this level of attrition means that our findings should be judged with caution.
The evidence from this study, while promising, requires corroboration in trials with higher retention.
Second, there were other social influences and media messages both pro-vaccination, and misinformation, related HPV during the time of our study.
Efforts were ongoing in Bauchi, and across Nigeria, to promote HPV vaccine uptake, and also unmeasured negative influences.
These may present important confounds to our study, and future research should examine their potential impact.
Third, this was not a randomized study, so while the heavy-up design provides a mechanism for causal inference, it has limitations.
For example, attention to and engagement with the campaign may be attributable to other factors that would influence the likelihood of HPV vaccine uptake.
Future studies should use randomized designs.
Finally, the nature of Meta's social media metrics prevents individual level attribution of campaign exposure to outcomes.
We have data on the exposure in the population, and can relate those metrics to our survey data, but not to individual study participants.
Social media campaigns show promise for HPV vaccination promotion.

There is a small, but growing body of evidence that social media can increase vaccination rates, and that higher levels of exposure to and engagement with such campaigns is associated with vaccine uptake.
These campaigns show evidence of producing high vaccine uptake at low cost.
Future research should use rigorous designs and examine specific factors (eg, the role of pro-vaccine attitudes and social norms) that may predict uptake.
